title: The king with ten heads
hook: Ravana weighs wise advice against his sister's rage; ahamkara, the ego
carry: ahamkara: the ego shouts over wisdom

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khara's army, and Rama, Vishnu come down, standing alone against fourteen thousand. And one survivor ran all the way to Lanka. Today, the king who's been waiting at the end of this story.

Lanka, the golden city. On the throne sits Ravana. Ten heads. Twenty arms. Before you picture a cartoon monster, hear what the tradition says about him. He's brilliant: a great scholar of the Vedas, a master musician, a devoted worshipper of Shiva. Once, the story goes, he tried to lift Shiva's mountain, got his arm pinned under it, and roared so loud that Shiva named him Ravana, the one who roars, or makes the world cry. A king of enormous power and enormous learning. And the messenger from the forest kneels in front of him: Khara is dead. His army is gone. One man did it. His name is Rama.
screen: `TEN HEADS, TWENTY ARMS.` → `SCHOLAR, MUSICIAN, DEVOTEE.` → `THE ONE WHO ROARS.` → `ONE MAN DID IT.`

segments.voice: The messenger adds a suggestion: you can't beat Rama in battle, but he has a wife, Sita, the most beautiful woman in the world. Take her, and he'll die of grief. Ravana likes the idea. He rides to an old rakshasa living as a hermit: Maricha. Maricha tells Ravana plainly: don't. Rama is not someone you want as an enemy. And, remarkably, Ravana listens. He goes home. It could have ended there. Then Shurpanakha walks into his court, disfigured and blazing. In Valmiki she doesn't just ask for revenge; she humiliates him in front of everyone. What kind of king are you, lying around in luxury while men cut up your sister and kill your army? Then she describes Sita. That does it. Notice what kind of mistake this is. Ravana isn't stupid. He heard the good advice and even followed it for a day. Hindu teaching has a name for what beat it: ahamkara, the ego. Literally, the I-maker: the part of you that makes everything about me, my honor, my insult. Some teachers read Ravana's ten heads as ten faults, anger, greed, pride and the rest, all talking at once. His learning didn't save him. The ego heard 'you've been insulted' louder than 'this is a terrible mistake'. That's why, at Dussehra, when huge effigies of Ravana go up in flames, many Hindus say they're burning something in themselves too.
screen: `TAKE HIS WIFE, THE MESSENGER SAYS.` · `MARICHA: DON'T.` · `SHURPANAKHA: WHAT KIND OF KING?` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · then, large: `AHAMKARA: THE EGO SHOUTS OVER WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Think of a time you knew the right thing and did the other thing because someone made you feel small. Give that voice its name: ahamkara, the I-maker. If you pray, offer it to God, the way Hindus give Ravana to the Dussehra fire. If not, just watch it for two minutes, and notice that the wise voice is quieter, and still there.
Ravana hears. The ten-headed king of Lanka ignores Maricha's warning and heeds his sister's rage, and decides to take Sita.
Your line: ahamkara, the ego shouts over wisdom. Ravana had heard the right voice first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Dussehra many Hindus burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana; many also remember him as a learned devotee of Shiva, and some communities honor him in their own ways.

Ravana.meaning: the ten-headed king of Lanka, learned and proud

Maricha.meaning: an old rakshasa hermit who warns Ravana to leave Rama alone

Shurpanakha.meaning: Ravana's sister, who shames him into seeking revenge

Vedas.meaning: the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism

Lanka.meaning: Ravana's island kingdom, across the ocean

Dussehra.meaning: the festival of Rama's victory, when Ravana effigies are burned
